items.stem: The bearing of B from X is 283°. What is the bearing of X from B?
The bearing of B from A is 254°. Omar says the bearing of A from B is 074° = 434°. Explain the mistake.
items.answer: Bearings are less than 360°. Since 254 > 180, subtract 180: the bearing of A from B is 074°.
items.markingKey: B1 cannot exceed 360°; B1 correct back bearing. [2]

items.stem: The bearing of B from A is 224°. Jonas says the bearing of A from B is 044° = 404°. Explain the mistake.
items.answer: Bearings are less than 360°. Since 224 > 180, subtract 180: the bearing of A from B is 044°.
items.markingKey: B1 cannot exceed 360°; B1 correct back bearing. [2]

items.stem: A map has a scale of 1 : 100,000. Two towns are 8.2 cm apart on the map. Work out the real distance between them in kilometres.
items.answer: 8.2 km

items.stem: A map has a scale of 1 : 100,000. Two towns are 12 cm apart on the map. Work out the real distance between them in kilometres.
items.answer: 12 km

items.stem: A boat leaves harbour H and sails 5 km due east to point B, then 5 km due south to point C. (a) Calculate the direct distance from C back to H, to 2 decimal places. (b) A scale drawing uses 1 cm to represent 2 km. How long is the line HB on the drawing? (c) Write down the bearing of B from H.
What is the three-figure bearing of the direction south?
items.markingKey: Measured clockwise from north: 180°. [1]

items.stem: The bearing of B from A is 230°. Hana says the bearing of A from B is 050° = 410°. Explain the mistake.
items.answer: Bearings are less than 360°. Since 230 > 180, subtract 180: the bearing of A from B is 050°.
items.markingKey: B1 cannot exceed 360°; B1 correct back bearing. [2]

items.stem: A plan of a classroom is drawn using a scale of 1 : 200. A wall is 6 m long. Explain how to work out the length of the wall on the plan, and give the answer in cm.
items.answer: Convert 6 m to 600 cm and divide by 200: 3 cm.
items.markingKey: B1 converts units; B1 divides by scale factor and gives value. [2]

items.stem: The bearing of B from A is 257°. Nadia says the bearing of A from B is 077° = 437°. Explain the mistake.
items.answer: Bearings are less than 360°. Since 257 > 180, subtract 180: the bearing of A from B is 077°.
items.markingKey: B1 cannot exceed 360°; B1 correct back bearing. [2]

items.stem: A ship sails from port P on a bearing of 223° to a lighthouse L. Work out the bearing it must sail on to return from L to P. Explain your method.
items.markingKey: The return is in the opposite direction, so subtract 180° (M1): 223 − 180 = 043° (A1).

items.stem: A plane flies on a bearing of 104°. It then turns 56° clockwise. Write down the new bearing, and the bearing that would take it straight back the way it has just come.
A boat leaves harbour H and sails 4 km due west to point B, then 4 km due north to point C. (a) Explain why angle BCH is 45°. (b) Work out the bearing of H from C.
items.answer: (a) Triangle HBC is right-angled at B and isosceles (HB = BC), so the other two angles are each 45°. (b) 135°

items.stem: A boat leaves harbour H and sails 5 km due east to point B, then 5 km due north to point C. (a) Explain why angle BCH is 45°. (b) Work out the bearing of H from C. (c) A scale drawing uses 1 cm to represent 2 km. How long is the line HB on the drawing?
items.answer: (a) Triangle HBC is right-angled at B and isosceles (HB = BC), so the other two angles are each 45°. (b) 225° (c) 2.5 cm

items.stem: What is the midpoint of the line segment from (−2, 0) to (10, −6)?
items.markingKey: Average the coordinates: (4, −3). [1]

items.stem: A is (2, 2) and B is (6, 10). Zara says the point that divides AB in the ratio 1 : 3 is the midpoint of A and the midpoint of AB. Is Zara correct? Explain.
items.answer: Yes. The midpoint of AB is half way; the midpoint of A and that point is 1/4 of the way, which is AP : PB = 1 : 3. P = (3, 4).
items.markingKey: B1 1/4 of the way; B1 coordinates. [2]

items.stem: Lina says the midpoint of (6, 2) and (7, 7) is (0.5, 2.5). Explain the mistake and give the correct midpoint.
items.answer: Lina halved the differences instead of averaging the coordinates. Midpoint = (6.5, 4.5).
items.markingKey: B1 add then halve; B1 correct midpoint. [2]

items.stem: M (1, 3) is the midpoint of AB. A is (0, −5). Find the coordinates of B.
Find the midpoint of AB where A is (−3, −4) and B is (0, 1).
ABCD is a parallelogram with A(0, −3), B(4, 1) and C(5, 9). (a) Find the midpoint of the diagonal AC. (b) Point P lies on AB so that AP : PB = 3 : 1. Find the coordinates of P.
items.markingKey: (a) M1; A1 [2] (b) M1 3/4 of the way; A1 [2]

items.stem: What is the midpoint of (0, 0) and (8, 6)?
items.markingKey: Halve each coordinate. [1]

items.stem: Arjun says the midpoint of (1, 4) and (10, 11) is (4.5, 3.5). Explain the mistake and give the correct midpoint.
items.answer: Arjun halved the differences instead of averaging the coordinates. Midpoint = (5.5, 7.5).
items.markingKey: B1 add then halve; B1 correct midpoint. [2]

items.stem: Tariq says (7, 6) is the midpoint of (5, 1) and (7, 11). Explain how to check this and say whether Tariq is right.
items.answer: The midpoint is ((5 + 7)/2, (1 + 11)/2) = (6, 6), so Tariq is wrong.
items.markingKey: M1 method; A1 conclusion. [2]

items.stem: A is (4, 5) and B is (8, 13). Priya says the point that divides AB in the ratio 1 : 3 is the midpoint of A and the midpoint of AB. Is Priya correct? Explain.
items.answer: Yes. The midpoint of AB is half way; the midpoint of A and that point is 1/4 of the way, which is AP : PB = 1 : 3. P = (5, 7).
items.markingKey: B1 1/4 of the way; B1 coordinates. [2]

items.stem: Find the midpoint of AB where A is (4, −4) and B is (4, 2).
A is (−6, −1) and B is (9, −6). Point P lies on AB so that AP : PB = 1 : 4. Find the coordinates of P.
items.markingKey: P is 1/5 of the way from A to B (M1); A + 1/5 × (15, −5) (M1) = (−3, −2) (A1).

items.stem: ABCD is a parallelogram with A(0, 2), B(6, 8) and C(5, 14). (a) Find the midpoint of the diagonal AC. (b) The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. Use this to find the coordinates of D.
items.markingKey: (a) M1; A1 [2] (b) M1 midpoint of BD = midpoint of AC; A1 [2]

items.stem: ABCD is a parallelogram with A(−3, 0), B(7, 2) and C(10, 8). (a) The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other. Use this to find the coordinates of D. items.markingKey: (a) M1 midpoint of BD = midpoint of AC; A1 [2] (b) M1 1/4 of the way from A; A1 [2] (c) M1 3/4 of the way; A1 [2]

items.stem: The point (6, −3) is transformed by a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of its image?
items.markingKey: Rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin: (6, −3) → (−3, −6). [1]

items.stem: Samuel reflects (6, 4) in the x-axis and gets (−6, 4). Explain the mistake.
items.answer: Reflecting in the x-axis keeps x the same and changes the sign of y: (6, −4). Samuel has reflected in the y-axis.
items.markingKey: B1 explanation; B1 correct image. [2]

items.stem: Mei reflects (1, 5) in the x-axis and gets (−1, 5). Explain the mistake.
items.answer: Reflecting in the x-axis keeps x the same and changes the sign of y: (1, −5). Mei has reflected in the y-axis.
items.markingKey: B1 explanation; B1 correct image. [2]

items.stem: Triangle A has vertices (3, 2), (3, 3), (5, 3). Write down the coordinates of the vertices of the image of triangle A after a reflection in the y-axis.
items.markingKey: Apply the rule to each vertex (M1); (−3, 2), (−3, 3), (−5, 3) (A1).

items.stem: Triangle P has vertices (3, 4), (2, 1), (5, 1). Triangle Q has vertices (−4, 3), (−1, 2), (−1, 5). Describe fully the single transformation that maps P onto Q.
items.answer: Rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin
items.markingKey: B1 type of transformation; B1 full detail (mirror line / angle, direction and centre / vector).

items.stem: Triangle T has vertices (1, 1), (5, 1), (1, 3). T is mapped onto triangle A by a reflection in the x-axis. Triangle A is then mapped onto triangle B by a rotation of 180° about the origin. (a) Write down the coordinates of the vertices of triangle A. (b) Explain why triangle B is congruent to triangle T. (c) Explain how to decide whether a single transformation maps T onto B.
items.answer: (a) (1, −1), (5, −1), (1, −3) (b) Reflections and rotations do not change lengths or angles. (c) Compare the coordinates of T and B and test a rule (e.g. reflection in y = x swaps coordinates).
items.markingKey: (a) B2 (B1 for two correct) [2] (b) B1 [1] (c) B1 [1]

items.stem: The point (1, 2) is transformed by a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin. What are the coordinates of its image?
items.markingKey: Rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin: (1, 2) → (−2, 1). [1]

items.stem: Chloe reflects (3, 6) in the x-axis and gets (−3, 6). Explain the mistake.
items.answer: Reflecting in the x-axis keeps x the same and changes the sign of y: (3, −6). Chloe has reflected in the y-axis.
items.markingKey: B1 explanation; B1 correct image. [2]

items.stem: A shape is transformed by a reflection in the line y = x followed by a reflection in the line y = x. Describe the single transformation that has the same effect. Check your answer with the point (3, 4).
items.answer: No change (the shape returns to where it started).

items.stem: Triangle A has vertices (5, 4), (3, 3), (2, 1). Write down the coordinates of the vertices of the image of triangle A after a rotation of 90° anticlockwise about the origin.
items.markingKey: Apply the rule to each vertex (M1); (−4, 5), (−3, 3), (−1, 2) (A1).

items.stem: Triangle P has vertices (3, 6), (2, 1), (6, 1). Triangle Q has vertices (−1, 9), (−2, 4), (2, 4). Describe fully the single transformation that maps P onto Q.
items.answer: Translation by the vector (−4, 3)
items.markingKey: B1 type of transformation; B1 full detail (mirror line / angle, direction and centre / vector).

items.stem: Triangle A has vertices (2, 1), (4, 1), (4, 2). Write down the coordinates of the vertices of the image of triangle A after a reflection in the line y = x.
items.markingKey: Apply the rule to each vertex (M1); (1, 2), (1, 4), (2, 4) (A1).

items.stem: Triangle T has vertices (1, 1), (4, 1), (1, 4). T is mapped onto triangle A by a reflection in the line y = −x. (b) Write down the coordinates of the vertices of triangle B. (c) Explain why triangle B is congruent to triangle T. (d) Explain how to decide whether a single transformation maps T onto B.
items.answer: (a) (−1, −1), (−1, −4), (−4, −1) (b) (1, −1), (4, −1), (1, −4) (c) Reflections and rotations do not change lengths or angles. (d) Compare the coordinates of T and B and test a rule (e.g. reflection in y = x swaps coordinates).
items.markingKey: (a) B2 (B1 for two correct) [2] (b) M1; A1 [2] (c) B1 [1] (d) B1 [1]

items.stem: A side of length 9 cm becomes 27 cm after an enlargement. What is the scale factor?
A rectangle with area 20 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 1/2. Samuel says the new area is 10 cm². Explain why Samuel is wrong and give the correct area.
items.answer: Both the length and the width are multiplied by 1/2, so the area is multiplied by 1/2² = 1/4: 5 cm².
items.markingKey: B1 area factor k²; B1 correct area. [2]

items.stem: A rectangle with area 10 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 3. Chloe says the new area is 30 cm². Explain why Chloe is wrong and give the correct area.

items.answer: Scale factor 3; centre (−1, −1)
items.markingKey: Compare corresponding lengths: scale factor 3 (B1); draw lines through corresponding vertices and find where they meet (M1); centre (−1, −1) (A1).

items.markingKey: Vector from centre to each vertex × 2 (M1); image (6, 3), (8, 3), (4, 1) (A1).

items.stem: A rectangle measures 6 cm by 2 cm. It is enlarged by scale factor 1/2. (a) Work out the dimensions of the image. (b) Work out the area of the image and compare it with the original area. (c) Explain why the angles of the image are the same as the angles of the original.
items.answer: (a) 3 cm by 1 cm (b) 3 cm²; 1/4 times the original 12 cm² (c) Enlargement keeps the shape the same (similar shapes); only the lengths change.

items.stem: A rectangle measures 6 cm by 2 cm. It is enlarged by scale factor 3. (a) Work out the perimeter of the image and compare it with the original perimeter. items.answer: (a) 48 cm; it is 3 times the original 16 cm (b) 108 cm²; 9 times the original 12 cm² (c) Enlargement keeps the shape the same (similar shapes); only the lengths change.

items.stem: A side of length 4 cm becomes 6 cm after an enlargement. What is the scale factor?

items.answer: Each length is halved

items.stem: Noah says that an enlargement always makes a shape bigger. Use an enlargement with scale factor 1/2 to explain why this is not true.

items.stem: Explain why the bearing of A from B and the bearing of B from A always differ by 180°.
items.answer: They are opposite directions along the same line, and opposite directions differ by half a turn, 180°.

items.stem: A shape is transformed by a translation by the vector (2, 3) followed by a translation by the vector (−5, 1). Describe the single transformation that has the same effect. Check your answer with the point (5, 5).
items.answer: Translation by the vector (−3, 4).
items.markingKey: B1 correct single transformation; B1 check with the point. [2]

items.stem: Triangle A has vertices (2, 4), (4, 4), (5, 3). Write down the coordinates of the vertices of the image of triangle A after a reflection in the y-axis.
items.markingKey: Apply the rule to each vertex (M1); (−2, 4), (−4, 4), (−5, 3) (A1).

items.stem: Triangle T has vertices (1, 1), (3, 1), (1, 2). T is mapped onto triangle A by a reflection in the line y = x. Triangle A is then mapped onto triangle B by a rotation of 90° clockwise about the origin. (a) Write down the coordinates of the vertices of triangle B. (b) Explain why triangle B is congruent to triangle T. (c) Explain how to decide whether a single transformation maps T onto B.
items.answer: (a) (1, −1), (3, −1), (1, −2) (b) Reflections and rotations do not change lengths or angles. (c) Compare the coordinates of T and B and test a rule (e.g. reflection in y = x swaps coordinates).

items.stem: A rectangle with area 20 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 1/2. Tariq says the new area is 10 cm². Explain why Tariq is wrong and give the correct area.
items.answer: Both the length and the width are multiplied by 1/2, so the area is multiplied by 1/2² = 1/4: 5 cm².
items.markingKey: B1 area factor k²; B1 correct area. [2]

items.stem: A rectangle with area 10 cm² is enlarged by scale factor 1/2. Lucas says the new area is 5 cm². Explain why Lucas is wrong and give the correct area.
items.answer: Both the length and the width are multiplied by 1/2, so the area is multiplied by 1/2² = 1/4: 5/2 cm².
items.markingKey: B1 area factor k²; B1 correct area. [2]

items.stem: Felix says that an enlargement always makes a shape bigger. Use an enlargement with scale factor 2/3 to explain why this is not true.
items.answer: With scale factor 2/3 (between 0 and 1) every length is multiplied by 2/3, so the image is smaller. It is still called an enlargement.
items.markingKey: B1 lengths × k < original; B1 conclusion. [2]

items.stem: Triangle A has vertices (2, 0), (3, 3), (2, 3). Triangle A is enlarged by scale factor 4 with centre the origin. Write down the coordinates of the image.
items.markingKey: Vector from centre to each vertex × 4 (M1); image (8, 0), (12, 12), (8, 12) (A1).

items.stem: Triangle P has vertices (2, 0), (4, 1), (3, 1). Triangle Q has vertices (3, 1), (7, 3), (5, 3). Q is an enlargement of P. Find the scale factor and the centre of enlargement.
items.answer: Scale factor 2; centre (1, −1)
items.markingKey: Compare corresponding lengths: scale factor 2 (B1); draw lines through corresponding vertices and find where they meet (M1); centre (1, −1) (A1).

items.stem: A rectangle measures 6 cm by 6 cm. It is enlarged by scale factor 3. (a) Work out the dimensions of the image. (b) Work out the perimeter of the image and compare it with the original perimeter. (c) Explain why the angles of the image are the same as the angles of the original.
items.answer: (a) 18 cm by 18 cm (b) 72 cm; it is 3 times the original 24 cm (c) Enlargement keeps the shape the same (similar shapes); only the lengths change.
